title: Computing sparse Hessian and Jacobian approximations with optimal hereditary properties
contribution: Estimates a sparse Hessian (or Jacobian) as the least-squares fit to all m recent quasi-Newton conditions via a constrained Procrustes problem, gives near-tight uniqueness conditions without a non-sparse-diagonal assumption, and solves the resulting system by matrix-free CG; preliminary tests show no gain over L-BFGS.
problem_entry: Dense quasi-Newton updates fill in, limited-memory updates ignore sparsity, and earlier sparse updates assume a non-sparse diagonal; seek a sparse B with B Gamma = Delta for the whole bundle of m difference pairs (pp. 2-3, 7).
key_idea: Constrained Procrustes problem min ||B Gamma - Delta||_F with symmetry and sparsity; KKT gives a Lyapunov-type equation, vectorized to a Kronecker-sum system reduced to the free lower-triangular entries, solved by warm-started inexact CG (pp. 3-5, 11-12).
assumptions: f in C2 or r in C1, symmetric sparsity pattern (p. 2); uniqueness needs the row-independence condition of Theorem 1 (p. 7); the converse needs a non-sparse diagonal and no LDL^T fill-in (p. 7).
proof_devices: Column-by-column contradiction showing K positive definite on the sparse symmetric space (Theorem 1, p. 7)
Null-vector construction from the largest dependent index j0, kept sparse by the no-fill-in assumption (Theorem 2, pp. 7-8)
Block-diagonal reduction giving an iff condition for the Jacobian case (Theorem 3, p. 10)
Three-variable tridiagonal example showing column independence of Gamma is not sufficient (p. 6)
experiments: Matlab trust-region code on chained Rosenbrock and a boundary value problem (n = 10, 100) against L-BFGS (m = 2, 5) and Newton; iterations, gradient and function calls; no improvement over L-BFGS, flop cost per iteration an order of magnitude higher (pp. 12-13).
positioning: Contrasted point by point with Toint (PSB-like, no quadratic termination), Fletcher 1995 (weighted norm, non-sparse diagonal) and Curtis-Powell-Reid / Powell-Toint (prescribed differencing directions, extra evaluations) (pp. 7, 9-10).
writing: Plain admission of disappointment in the conclusion, with the reason the comparison meter is rough (p. 13).
limits_future: No obvious sparsity in P^T K P, Theorem 1 hard to verify, disappointing numerics; future: make it efficient and embed it in a trust-region SQP (pp. 11, 13).

method_links.note: Reports that the new method does not beat L-BFGS and flags that iteration counts are only a rough meter because iteration costs differ
Small worked example marks the edge of a sufficient condition (column independence fails to ensure definiteness)
Weak: the stated next step is to carry the update into an SQP method

transferable: When per-iteration costs differ, say iteration counts give only a rough comparison and report flops per iteration alongside (p. 13).
Warm-start the inner iterative solve from the previous outer iterate's answer and tighten its tolerance as the outer method converges (p. 11).
Pair a sufficient condition with a near-necessary one under a stated structural assumption, plus a tiny example where the weaker condition fails (pp. 6-8).

quotes.text: Overall, we have been rather disappointed by these preliminary experiments
It should not come as a surprise that Newton's method is the best of the three methods since it utilizes the most problem information (exact Hessian) of the three methods.

title: Comparison of certain MINLP algorithms when applied to a model structure determination and parameter estimation problem
contribution: Formulates joint model-structure selection and parameter estimation (AIC minimization) for FTIR calibration as a convex MIQP inside a covariance-relaxation loop and compares OA, ECP and QP-based B&B, finding opposite rankings by CPU time and by function evaluations.
problem_entry: Application-driven: AIC minimization with binary switches per parameter is an MINLP; FTIR instance with up to 16,800 variables reduced to 600 and 1,200 (pp. 1-3, 7-8).
key_idea: Solve the convex known-covariance objective J1 repeatedly and re-estimate the covariance in an outer relaxation loop instead of attacking the nonconvex J2; compare three convex-MINLP algorithms on it (pp. 4-6).
assumptions: Linear model, normal i.i.d. residuals, convexity for OA/ECP global optimality (p. 5); the covariance relaxation has no convergence proof (p. 4).
experiments: Two FTIR instances; bound curves versus CPU time and versus function evaluations (Figs 2-6); B&B fastest in CPU (15 s vs 60 s OA, 480 s ECP) but ECP fewest evaluations (65 vs ~2000, ~6000); B&B counts Hessian-vector products as a proxy (pp. 8-11).
positioning: Places OA (Duran-Grossmann), ECP (Westerlund-Pettersson) and Fletcher-Leyffer MIQP B&B as interchangeable convex-MINLP solvers and does not crown one (pp. 5-6, 12).
writing: Conclusion by bottleneck profile rather than winner; all methods 'can be recommended' (p. 12).
limits_future: One application class; nonconvex J2 not treated; relaxation unproved (pp. 4, 12).

method_links.note: Two meters with opposite rankings, a caveat on the B&B proxy counter, conclusion by bottleneck not winner
Chooses the convex J1 formulation and moves the nonconvexity into an outer re-estimation loop
Indirect: the model reappears as a large convex MIQP application in S039 (S039 p. 2)

transferable: Plot bounds against two meters (CPU time and function evaluations) and say which bottleneck each exposes (pp. 8-9, 12).
When a solver cannot report the shared meter, name the proxy counted and what else it includes (p. 9).
Fix a nuisance parameter that makes the problem nonconvex, solve the convex problem globally, and update the parameter in an outer loop, stating that loop is unproved (p. 4).

quotes.text: In the case of the QPbased B&B method it is not possible to count function evaluations separately.
The ECP spends most of the time in solving the MILP, while the B&B again spends most time in solving the non-linear functions.

title: On the Global Convergance of an SLP-Filter Algorithm
A bundle filter method for nonsmooth nonlinear optimization
contribution: Replaces the exact penalty in Kiwiel-type constrained bundle methods by a filter with envelope, giving an SLP trust-region bundle-filter method for convex nonsmooth constrained problems with a global convergence proof to nonsmooth Fritz-John points.
problem_entry: Nonsmooth convex constrained problems arising as Benders master problems (stochastic NLP); Kiwiel's penalty approach suffers from subgradients of widely varying magnitude (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Keep the bundle LP with trust region; accept steps by a tilted-envelope filter with f-type/h-type sufficient reduction, null steps to enrich the bundle, and a restoration phase (pp. 4-9).
assumptions: A1 bounded polyhedral X; A2 convex locally Lipschitz f, c; A3 one arbitrary subgradient per point (pp. 1-2); single constraint, extension asserted (p. 2).
proof_devices: Nonsmooth Fritz-John conditions by contradiction via upper semicontinuity and the mean-value theorem (Lemma 2.1, p. 3)
Finite inner iteration by rescaling the LP by rho to a rho-independent LP over the tangent cone (Lemma 4.1, pp. 9-10)
Null steps change the LP by at least sigma2*Delta_l or beta*tau (Remark 4.2, pp. 10-11)
Four-case split A-D with one lemma per case (p. 11; Lemmas 4.3-4.5, Theorem 4.6, pp. 11-15)
LP consistency for rho in an interval [h/eps, kappa] via Lipschitz bound on shifted cuts (Lemma 4.4, pp. 12-13)
positioning: Closest to Kiwiel 1987, differing only in the globalization; cites the smooth filter papers and Audet-Dennis pattern-search filter (pp. 2, 6).
writing: Short report; advantages of filters asserted in the introduction (no penalty parameter, beneficial nonmonotonicity) without numbers (p. 2).
limits_future: No numerical results; feasibility lemma relies on an unpublished Chin-Fletcher report (NA/XXX); multi-constraint case and restoration only sketched (pp. 2, 9, 11, 15).

method_links.note: Home device (filter) carried into nonsmooth constrained optimization in place of the field's penalty; theory before numbers here, contrary to Heuristic 3

transferable: To carry a globalization device into a new class, keep the class's standard model (bundle LP) intact and swap only the acceptance test (pp. 4-7).
To prove an inner loop finite as the trust region shrinks, rescale the subproblem by the radius so its solution becomes radius-independent (pp. 9-10).
Organize a convergence proof by an exhaustive case split on the iteration's long-run behaviour, one lemma per case (p. 11).

quotes.text: Instead the novel concept of a filter [6] is used to force global convergence.
Filter methods have several advantages over penalty function methods.

title: A note on feasibility in Benders decomposition
contribution: Gives a three-variable convex NLP on which Benders decomposition with standard feasibility cuts converges to a feasible non-stationary point, checks it against the hypotheses of the published convergence theorems, and repairs the method with a relaxed-subproblem optimality cut, admitting a residual gap in the proof.
problem_entry: Published Benders convergence needs finite Y, all subproblems feasible, or finite dual sets, none of which hold for general NLP (p. 3); counterexample (P1) with two circles of radius sqrt(ln y) (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Feasibility cuts carry no objective information; when S(y) is infeasible also solve an enlarged NLP with constraints relaxed to m1*c+ (Slater holds) and add its optimality cut (pp. 6-7).
assumptions: A1 convex C2 f, c; A2 compact polyhedral X, Y; A3 Slater (p. 2).
proof_devices: Closed-form Benders recursion y(k+1) = (2 - ln y(k)) y(k) < e via substitution y = e*gamma and monotonicity (Lemma 2.1, p. 5)
Hypothesis check against Geoffrion Thm 2.5 and Flippo-Rinnooy Kan Thm 3.3 before claiming an error (section 2.1, p. 5)
Underestimating cut from aggregating outer-approximation linearizations with KKT multipliers and normal-cone element (Lemma 3.4, p. 9)
Bounded multipliers from Slater on the enlarged problem (Lemma 3.1, p. 8; Theorem 3.1, pp. 9-10)
positioning: Does not call Geoffrion or Flippo-Rinnooy Kan wrong: their assumptions exclude the example; relevance extended to bundle-based decomposition (pp. 5, 10).
writing: Section 3.2 retains working-note voice ('This is Roger's approach', 'I am not sure...', a rhetorical question about decomposition) inside a numbered report (pp. 11-12).
limits_future: Theorem 3.1 only excludes values above f* + eps1*m, and eps1*m can be O(1) (Remarks 3.1, 3.3, pp. 8, 10); penalty and augmented-Lagrangian alternatives left open (pp. 11-12).

method_links.note: Smallest convex counterexample, hypothesis check before claiming an error, redesign of the infeasible-subproblem step; the canonical case [03 E44]
Failure traced to how infeasible subproblems are formulated, not to Benders as such

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Admit the residual gap of your own theorem in print
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Remark 3.3 states the proof only excludes f-hat > f* + eps1*m and that this can be O(1); working notes on open alternatives left in the report

transferable: Build the counterexample so the iteration has a closed-form recursion and prove the limit with a one-variable monotonicity argument (pp. 4-5).
After a counterexample, check it against each cited theorem's hypotheses and name the violated one (p. 5).
State what your convergence theorem does not exclude and how large the residual gap can be (p. 10).
coauthors: Andreas Grothey, Ken I. M. McKinnon

quotes.text: At a first glance, the example seems to indicate that there are errors in the various convergence results in the literature.
Is this maybe an argument against decomposition (at least at the NLP level)?

title: Solving large MINLPs on computational grids
contribution: Parallelizes SQP-based nonlinear branch-and-bound on a Condor grid with a master-worker scheme whose tasks are MINLP subtrees, with time limits, a recourse period and lazy best-first search, reaching up to 80% parallel efficiency on large MacMINLP instances.
problem_entry: Large MINLPs with B&B trees up to 10^9 NLPs; computational grids of idle, heterogeneous, unreliable machines; MINLP-specific issues beyond parallel MILP (pp. 1-3, 13-14).
key_idea: Task = MINLP subtree searched depth-first by a sequential filterSQP B&B worker, not a single NLP (which was too fast for the master); time limit plus recourse period to fathom small-gap nodes; lazy best-first with pool-size hysteresis at the master (pp. 8-10).
assumptions: Compact X, Y; f, g twice continuously differentiable; no convexity assumed, global optimality only if each NLP is solved globally (pp. 2, 4).
experiments: 146 Condor machines, 10 MacMINLP problems; parallel efficiency (not speed-up, with reasons) up to 80%, mostly over 40%; trimlon7 ~10^9 NLPs; non-monotone lower bound on nonconvex trimlon7 reported (pp. 12-16).
positioning: Differentiated from parallel MILP work (Eckstein CM-5, Chen-Ferris FATCOP, Laursen) and from OA/Benders, which need synchronization and two task types (pp. 3, 6).
writing: Headline 'up to two orders of magnitude' faster than serial (pp. 14, 16), while Table 3 work-time/job-time ratios are at most about 66 (my computation, p. 13).
limits_future: No guarantee on nonconvex instances; future: early branching (faster but less reliable on nonconvex problems) and parallel cut generation (pp. 4, 16-17).

method_links.note: Own C++ B&B with pluggable NLP solver designed around filterSQP warm starts and feasibility-problem infeasibility detection
Test set from his MacMINLP collection, AMPL models online
Meter choice justified (efficiency, not speed-up), but the 'two orders of magnitude' headline exceeds the Table 3 ratios

Normalize heterogeneous workers with a benchmark task run on joining (p. 11).
List the inner-solver requirements the outer tree imposes (robust under degeneracy, reliable infeasibility detection, warm starts) before choosing the inner solver (p. 5).

title: The penalty interior point method fails to converge for mathematical programs with equilibrium constraints
contribution: Constructs a three-variable MPEC satisfying strict complementarity and nonsingularity on which PIPA converges to a non-stationary point, confirms it by an AMPL run, and traces the failure to a trust-region radius tied to infeasibility, with a detectable multiplier symptom.
problem_entry: Counterexample to the published PIPA convergence theorem under [SC] and [NS] (Luo-Pang-Ralph Thm 6.1.17) (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: The direction-finding bound ||dx||^2 <= rho(||F|| + y'w) shrinks as complementarity halves each step, so x moves only by a convergent geometric sum and stalls at a non-stationary limit (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: Those of the theorem under test, [SC] and [NS], verified at the solution and at the spurious limit; simplified PIPA with fixed parameters (pp. 2-3, 6).
proof_devices: Closed-form LP basis and multipliers of the direction-finding problem (pp. 3-4)
Step-size bound 5/9 <= alpha <= 1 via a Maple series expansion in w (p. 4)
Induction y(k+1)w(k+1) <= y(k)w(k)/2 and geometric-sum bounds on x and y (pp. 4-6)
Armijo acceptance and penalty never increased (p. 5); compactness gives a limit point satisfying [SC], [NS] (p. 6)
experiments: PIPA and the example coded with AMPL's looping extension; 10 iterates with actual and predicted reductions tabulated, confirming the bounds (p. 6).
positioning: Directed at Luo-Pang-Ralph's PIPA; Pang thanked for reading an earlier version (pp. 1, 7).
writing: Hedged in conclusion ('seems to contradict', p. 7) after 'contradicting Theorem 1.1' (pp. 2, 6); no faulty proof step located in this version.
limits_future: Diagnosis: radius should reflect model agreement, not feasibility; symptom: multiplier of the radius constraint tends to 1 (p. 7). Remedy not developed here.

method_links.note: Smallest instance, hypotheses checked as satisfied, run in AMPL, symptom and cause named
This 2002 report stops at 'seems to contradict'; pointing to the faulty proof step (step 3) appears only in the later version [03 E45], after Pang read a draft

transferable: Prove the counterexample analytically, then run it in a modelling language and tabulate iterates with actual and predicted reductions (p. 6).
End a failure report with a detectable symptom, e.g. a non-vanishing multiplier on the offending constraint (p. 7).
To break a method, look for a step or radius bound tied to the iterates rather than controlled by the algorithm (p. 7).

quotes.text: This paper presents a small example for whih the Penalty Interior Point Method onverges to a non-stationary point.

title: Large Scale Nonconvex Optimization (SIAG/Optimization Views-and-News issue, editors)
contribution: Guest-edited newsletter issue (with Nocedal) framing large-scale nonconvex optimization as NLP methods extending into DAE/PDE-constrained problems, MPCC and MINLP, with Leyffer's own MPCC survey (S057) inside.
problem_entry: Editors' framing: the SQP/AL versus interior-method competition revitalized NLP; its methods now reach DAE/PDE, MPCC and MINLP, the last 'a wide open field' (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Curated tour from the NLP core outward with an explicit invitation to branch out (p. 2); his article overturns the 'numerically unsafe' verdict on MPCCs as NLPs (pp. 15-16).
experiments: n/a (his article reports others' numbers: SQP on 150+ MPCCs, IPMs ~80% with defaults, pp. 16-17)
positioning: Introduction summarizes each contribution neutrally; his article positions NLP solvers against special-purpose MPCC methods (pp. 1-2, 15-16).
writing: Two-paragraph framing signed by both editors (p. 2); the editor's thanks (p. 25) are Sturm's voice.
limits_future: Editorial service, not research; open questions in his article: global convergence, B-stationarity, C-stationary points (p. 18).

method_links.note: Editors frame the field as NLP expertise carried outward into MPCC, MINLP, DAE/PDE; his article re-casts MPCCs as NLPs

transferable: When guest-editing a thematic issue, write the introduction as a map from one core competence to neighbouring classes, one article each, and close with an invitation to branch out (pp. 1-2).
